_doc: Registration of the National Archives / Historic Urban Plans facsimile of Wright's 1834 survey (source id wright_1834_nara_hup) IN ITS OWN PIXEL SPACE, beside the BPL master this project already traces (data/traces/gcp/wright_1834_gcps.json). Pixel coordinates here are coordinates of chicago/pre_fire_v1/maps/images/1834-wright-map.jpg, 5050 x 6628 px. They are NOT BPL coordinates and the two must never be mixed: the scan-to-scan block below gives the transform and its residuals. T-0787.

raster.note: The working copy lives outside this app's subtree, in chicago/pre_fire_v1/, where the owner placed it. This file cites it by path and checksum; it does not copy it.

sheet_caption.transcribed: 2026-09-06 from the printed caption at the foot of the sheet (NA pixels x 500..4800, y 6120..6400), read with tesseract and corrected against the image
columns: This reproduction is of James Wright's manuscript survey of Chicago in 1834. It was used in preparing one of the two earliest printed maps of the city published in that year. The original drawing is now in the collection of the National Archives in Washington, D.C.

Signs of wear are apparent. Two portions are missing, the larger being near the lower center. At one time the drawing was torn to this spot from the upper right margin. Later the manuscript was mounted on cloth to repair this tear and to prevent further damage.

The map shows the location of Fort Dearborn on the south bank of the Chicago River, a site now within the right-of-way of Michigan Avenue. To the left, bordered in red, is the original townsite surveyed by James Thompson in 1830.

From this modest beginning as a frontier settlement the modern metropolis began to evolve. The basic pattern of gridiron streets was repeated almost endlessly as the city expanded beyond the area shown on this unique document.
sheet_caption.imprint: Reproduced by HISTORIC URBAN PLANS, Ithaca, New York

relation_to_wright_1834: Same drawing, different scan, different pixel space. The BPL/Leventhal copy (commonwealth:js957744g, 4204 x 5166) remains the master for every trace already committed; this sheet is registered beside it so that readings made at 600 dpi can be cited. Neither is a second witness to the other: they are two photographs of one manuscript.
control_choice: BOTH, and the ticket asked which and why (T-0787). The eight control crossings are the SAME eight the BPL set uses, so the two fits are directly comparable — that is the first block below. A scan-to-scan affine is fitted as well, because the readings this sheet exists for (block numerals) have to be carried back to traces already keyed to BPL pixels — that is the second block.
method: Each control point was located by normalised cross-correlation of a 400 x 400 px patch cut from the BPL scan at that GCP against the NA sheet, over a scale sweep of 0.97-1.03, in a window centred on the prediction of a five-point affine. Because the patch is centred on the BPL pick, the match centre is the SAME point of the drawing, whatever picking convention the BPL set used — the correspondence does not depend on re-deciding what 'the crossing' means. Seven of the eight matched within 13 px of the affine and are taken as picked. G4 did not: its correlation peak ran to the edge of the search window, and a wider search found a peak 172 px away, which the block grid's ~145 px pitch makes an aliasing candidate. G4 was therefore picked by hand off a 20 px grid at 4x on both scans, from the same two ruled lines (block 38's west border and the Public Square block's south border), and carries a larger uncertainty. Estimated picking precision: +/- 5 px on the seven, +/- 8 px on G4.
control_source: Modern control from OpenStreetMap via the Overpass API, fetched 2026-08-09. Multi-node crossings averaged (max spread 6.4 m). OSM data is (c) OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL — see data/sources/osm_streets_2026.json.

fit.type: affine, least squares, NA pixel -> EPSG:26916

compared_with_wright_1834.finding: THE X SCALES AGREE AND THE Y SCALES DO NOT, which is what a different mounting of the same paper should look like. Across the sheet the two fits differ by 0.03% in x (0.6985 against 0.6983 m/px) and by 1.5% in y (0.7358 against 0.7246). The NA sheet's own x/y anisotropy is 5.2% where the BPL sheet's is 3.7%; the extra stretch is in the long axis, along which the manuscript was torn and backed. Fit quality is marginally better on the new scan (RMS 16.2 m against 17.5 m) on identical control, so nothing about this sheet argues for demoting it; the two fits' rotations are 1.894 deg here against 1.183 deg on the BPL sheet, a difference of 0.71 deg.

scan_to_scan.type: affine, least squares, BPL pixel -> NA pixel, all eight points

max_departure.note: Clark and Washington, at the south-east corner of the Public Square, is where the two scans disagree most. It is also the worst point of the BPL fit against modern control (32.7 m), which that file attributes to visible local warp in the sheet around the square. Two independent measurements now say the same thing about the same place: THE RESIDUAL IS THE FINDING, not a picking error.

scan_to_scan.warning: Applying this to carry a reading between the scans costs the residual above; it is not a lossless change of coordinates.

scale_bar.drawn: Scale of feet — 1200 / 600 / 300, subdivided 200 / 100 / 50 at the right end, at the foot of the sheet
scale_bar.method: tick columns found as darkness maxima of the column profile across the bar's ruled band, then a least-squares fit of pixel against feet
scale_bar.finding: THE BAR CORROBORATES THE HORIZONTAL FIT ON BOTH SHEETS AND SAYS NOTHING ABOUT THE VERTICAL, which is where the disagreement actually is. The bar is drawn horizontally, so it can only be compared with the fits' x scale: 0.6924 against 0.6985 m/px here (0.87%) and 0.6899 against 0.6983 on the BPL sheet (1.2%). Carried across the ~1750 px width of the plat that is 11 m and 12 m — inside each fit's own RMS (16.2 m and 17.5 m), so under this ticket's test it is a rounding and not a finding. The 5.2% and 3.7% x/y anisotropies are larger than either, and the bar cannot adjudicate them.

lacunae._doc: Paper the sheet has lost. Anything inside these boxes is cloth backing, not Wright, and no reading may be taken from them. Boxes are NA pixel space, [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max].
lacunae.method: Whole-sheet sweep inside the neat line for connected regions brighter than 200/255 with saturation below 0.14 — the cloth's tone, which no part of the aged paper reaches — then the bounding box of each region re-measured at full resolution. Two were found, which is the number the printed caption gives.

found.what_it_covers: The 'larger portion, near the lower center' of the caption. It sits on the east bank of the South Branch across the Reserved blocks numbered 87 and 88, and takes with it the west edge of that tier and part of the bank line.
A second, far smaller loss of the same tone, on the west edge of the Reserved strip beside the block numbered 49, taking a few millimetres of the block boundary with it.
found.note: The caption says two portions are missing and this is the only other white loss the sweep finds inside the neat line, so it is read as the second. It was not identified from the caption, which locates only the larger, and a reading that finds a better candidate should replace it.

lacunae.tear: The caption says the drawing 'was torn to this spot from the upper right margin' and was later mounted on cloth. The tear itself is repaired and no paper is missing along it, so it is not boxed; the upper right margin is blank sheet in this scan and carries no map content.
